Policy Research State of Working Maine 2026: Protecting Workers from Artificial Intelligence

State of Working Maine 2026 examines how artificial intelligence could reshape workplaces across the state and calls on policymakers to ensure technological change benefits workers, not just powerful corporations and investors.

The report places AI development in historical context, assesses exposure across Maine occupations and regions, and identifies practical steps to safeguard workers and share the benefits of technological progress. The finding is AI’s future effects remain uncertain, but the risks are familiar: job displacement, weakened worker power, intrusive surveillance, discrimination, and widening inequality.

State of Working Maine 2026 suggests Maine does not need to predict AI’s exact trajectory to act and urges Maine lawmakers to pair innovation with accountability. Lawmakers can set clear rules now so workers share in productivity gains, corporations pay their fair share of taxes, and no handful of companies or individuals gains too much power over wages, working conditions, public policy, or the economy.

Exposure does not automatically mean job loss. AI may complement workers, replace tasks or jobs, or raise profits without increasing pay. Policy choices will determine who benefits.

Disruption may be concentrated. There is no evidence yet of broad AI-driven unemployment in Maine, but technology firms, call centers, early-career workers, and particular communities show warning signs.

Unchecked AI could deepen inequality. Productivity gains may flow disproportionately to owners and investors, especially when workers lack bargaining power.

Corporate control creates workplace risks. AI-enabled surveillance, biased employment decisions, algorithmic wage-setting, worker-data misuse, and digital replicas can erode privacy and accountability.

Historic transitions show the need to act early. Even when technological change benefits the economy overall, displaced workers and communities can face severe and lasting harm.
